name: Virtual Location Scouting
title: Virtual Location Scouting
answer: Virtual location scouting is the practice of finding, generating, or assembling a plausible place for a shoot before anyone travels there. It covers real locations previewed through satellite and street imagery, digital reconstructions of places that exist, and wholly synthetic environments built to stand in for a place that does not. In photography and hyper-realist work it serves two purposes at once: planning a real shoot, and producing the final backdrop itself.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a mix of mapping and imagery services, 3D engines, and generative image tools. A scout may pull terrain and street-level views, drop a rough blockout into a real-time engine to test camera angles and light, then hand the result to an image generator for a finished plate. Because the site tracks 1,000 live image generation models, the choice of model is itself part of the setup, since each renders materials, foliage, and atmosphere differently.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical pass starts with a brief: era, region, weather, time of day, and the lens the shot needs. The scout gathers reference, builds or generates candidate views, and iterates on framing until the composition reads correctly at the intended crop. Hyper-realist work adds a second loop, checking that shadows, reflections, and surface wear stay consistent across every angle the scene will be seen from. The output is usually a set of approved views plus notes on camera position, focal length, and lighting.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions attach to both halves of the practice. Real locations carry property, access, and sometimes publicity considerations, and synthetic ones carry the provenance of whatever imagery trained the model. With 92 active intellectual property lawsuits tracked on this site, a scout should be able to say where each element of a scene came from and keep that record with the project. This is a description of common practice, not legal advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect scouting tools to fold mapping, 3D blockout, and generation into fewer steps, with scene state carried between them rather than rebuilt each time. Consistency across angles and lighting is the main technical gap, and closing it would make synthetic locations usable for full sequences rather than single frames. The open question is provenance, since a scene assembled from many sources needs a traceable record to survive review.
